title: The Rise in Importance of the Domestic Chicken

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The rise in importance of the domestic chicken is an epic story of evolutionary, agricultural, and culinary success, resulting in chickens now outnumbering human beings on the planet by nearly three to one. Chicken is the ubiquitous food of our era, crossing multiple cultural boundaries with ease. With its mild taste and uniform texture, chicken presents a conveniently bland base to which can be added flavors from almost any cuisine. How the chicken achieved its culinary dominance is surprising. Many archaeologists believe that chickens were first domesticated not for eating, but as sacred birds valued as benevolent spirits that crowed at dawn to herald a turning point in the cosmic struggle between day and night. In fact until the arrival of large-scale industrial production in the 20th century, the global economic and nutritional contribution of chickens was quite modest.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The chicken’s wild relative is the red junglefowl, Gallus gallus. In its habitat, which stretches from northeastern India to the Philippines, G. gallus browses on the forest floor for insects, seeds, and fruit, and flies up to nest in the trees at night. That is about as much flying as it can achieve, a trait that had obvious appeal to humans seeking to capture and raise it. This trait would lead to the later popularity of chickens in Africa, where the native guinea fowls have an annoying habit of flying away from farms into the forest.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In around 750 BC, Egyptians mastered the technique of artificial incubation, which meant that hens no longer had to hatch their eggs, and consequently had time to lay more of them. It was not an easy procedure. The Egyptians understood that most chicken eggs will hatch in three weeks, but only if the temperature is kept constant. The temperature has to be 37 to 40 degrees Celsius and the relative humidity close to 55 percent, increasing in the last few days of incubation. The eggs must also be turned three to five times a day, to avoid the possibility of physical deformities. The Egyptians constructed vast incubation complexes made up of hundreds of incubation chambers. Each was connected to a series of corridors and air vents that allowed attendants to circulate the heat from fires fueled by straw and camel dung. The egg attendants kept their methods a secret from outsiders for centuries.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Chickens were a delicacy among the Romans, whose culinary innovations included the practice of stuffing chickens for cooking. Roman farmers began developing methods to fatten and increase the size of the birds – some used wheat bread soaked in wine, while others preferred a mixture of cumin seeds, barley, and lizard fat. At one point, the authorities outlawed these practices out of concern about the pursuit of excessive luxury in the Roman Republic. A law in 161 BC limited the consumption of chicken.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: But the chicken’s status in Europe appears to have diminished with the collapse of the Roman Empire. Kevin MacDonald, a professor of archaeology at University College London, says, ‘In the post-Roman period, the size of chickens returned to what it was during the Iron Age,’ more than 1,000 years earlier. He speculates that the big, organized farms of Roman times, which were well suited to feeding numerous chickens and protecting them from predators, largely vanished. As the centuries went by, hardier fowls such as geese and partridge began to appear on medieval tables.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Like most animals, chickens need sunlight to synthesize vitamin D, and so in the first decades of the 20th century, they typically spent their days wandering around the farmyard, pecking for food. Today’s quarter-million-bird chicken farms were made possible by the fortification of grain with antibiotics, which meant that chickens could be raised indoors, out of the rain and snow and away from predators. Now, they are fed a controlled diet in a restricted environment designed to present the minimum of distractions from the essential business of eating. Chickens frequently have little quality of life; instead, they have become cogs in a system designed to convert grain into protein with staggering efficiency. It takes less than two pounds (0.90 kilo) of feed to produce one pound (0.45 kilo) of chicken meat. By comparison, it is more costly to produce a pound (0.45 kilo) of beef, as around seven pounds (3.175 kilos) of feed is needed.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In 2004, an international team of geneticists produced a complete map of the ‘chicken genome’, and they are the first descendants of dinosaurs to have received this honor. The genome map provided an excellent opportunity to study how millennia of domestication can alter a species. In a project based at Uppsala University, Sweden, scientists have been looking into the differences between the red junglefowl and its contemporary descendants. The scientists found important mutations in a gene which regulates glucose metabolism. In people, mutations in this gene have been associated with obesity, but it’s a desirable trait in a creature destined for the dinner table.

groups.title: Chicken farming today
content: Chickens on many modern chicken farms do not have the freedom to move around fields and farmyards to find their own food. They are now kept {{22}} , where they are not affected by adverse weather conditions and are no longer in danger of attack from predators. Chickens used to have access to {{23}} , which provided them with vitamin D. It is no longer necessary for them to be outside because the grain they eat has been strengthened by the addition of {{24}} . This results in a food source for humans high in {{25}} . The effectiveness of the modern farming process means that chicken meat can be produced much more cheaply than {{26}} .
